sections.h2: Where is New Rochelle and what kind of city is it?
sections.html:
New Rochelle is a Westchester County city on Long Island Sound, about 17 miles from Midtown Manhattan and two miles north of the Bronx line at Pelham Bay Park. It is long and narrow, roughly 10 miles from north to south and about 1.5 miles across at its widest point, with 10.29 square miles of land and another 2.86 square miles of water.

The city shares borders with Pelham, Pelham Manor, Eastchester, Scarsdale, Mamaroneck and Larchmont. For a seller, that means a house a few blocks apart can sit in a very different setting: a dense downtown near the train, a tree-lined single-family street, or a waterfront neighborhood on Davenport Neck.

The Census Bureau counted 79,726 people in 2020 and estimates 85,864 for July 1, 2025, a gain of 7.7 percent over the 2020 estimates base.

sections.h2: What is the history behind New Rochelle's housing?
sections.html:
The city traces back to 1688, when about 33 families, many of them artisans from La Rochelle in France, founded a Huguenot settlement on land that Thomas Pell had bought from the Siwanoy in 1654. The village was set up in 1857, and the village and town merged into one city under a charter signed in 1899.

Planned residential districts such as Rochelle Park, one of the first planned communities in the country, earned New Rochelle the nickname "City of Homes." The result is a mix of ages on one block. Older neighborhoods lean Queen Anne, Tudor Revival and Colonial Revival, while the southwest quarter has brownstones, townhomes and mid-rise buildings.

Age matters when you sell. A house from the early 1900s often has old wiring, original windows or an unpermitted porch enclosure, and those are the details a buyer's inspector will find first.

sections.h2: How big is the housing market in New Rochelle?
sections.html:
It is a large one for a city this size: more than 11,500 single-family houses, plus a downtown of condominiums, high rises and affordable housing complexes. The Census Bureau lists 31,684 households for 2020 to 2024, and only 53.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied.

That renter share is worth knowing if you own a two-family or have a tenant in place. The median gross rent was $1,917 in the same period, and the median value of an owner-occupied home was $702,500.

  • Median household income: $109,167 (2020 to 2024, in 2024 dollars)
  • Average commute: 32.5 minutes each way
  • Residents with a bachelor's degree or higher: 51.6 percent
  • Foreign-born residents: 29.5 percent

The city lists named neighborhoods including Wykagyl, Beechmont, Rochelle Heights, Residence Park, Paine Heights, Larchmont Woods, Bonnie Crest, Glenwood Lake and Davenport Neck. A few, such as Premium Point and Pinebrook Hollow, are gated.

sections.h2: What do the roads, train and schools mean for a seller in New Rochelle?
sections.html:
Commuter access is the strongest selling point most New Rochelle houses have. The Metro-North New Haven Line and Amtrak's Northeast Regional both stop at the downtown station, and Interstate 95 has four exits inside the city. The Hutchinson River Parkway is passenger-vehicle only and backs up in both directions at rush hour, while the Boston Post Road works as Main Street through downtown.

The City School District of New Rochelle runs one high school, two middle schools, six elementary schools and an early childhood center. Confirm with the district which school your street feeds before you list. Higher education adds a steady local population: Iona University, Mercy University's New Rochelle campus (the former College of New Rochelle) and Monroe College.

Westchester County Airport serves the county, and the New York City airports are an easy drive.

sections.h2: What do I owe in property tax on a New Rochelle house, and when?
sections.html:
You pay four separate tax bills a year, and a sale in the middle of a cycle has to be split at closing. The city bill covers January 1 to December 31 and is due by January 31, the county bill is due by June 30, and school and library taxes are due in two halves on September 30 and March 31.

DateNew Rochelle tax or assessment step
December 1Taxable status date and exemption application deadline
January 31City property tax due
February 1Tentative assessment roll
Third Tuesday in FebruaryGrievance Day
March 31Second half of school and library tax due
April 1Final assessment roll
June 30County property tax due
September 30First half of school and library tax due

Source: the City of New Rochelle assessment and property tax schedule pages. Payments after the end of the collection month pick up interest and penalties.

One local fact stands out: the city has not run a citywide reassessment since 1956. Instead, any addition or renovation is reviewed as of the December 1 taxable status date and shows up on the tentative roll the next February. If you finished a big project this year, your buyer may see a higher bill than yours.

sections.h2: How do I record the sale and change the owner of record?
sections.html:
The deed is recorded with the Westchester County Clerk, not at City Hall. New Rochelle's assessor says ownership records cannot be changed at the city level and points owners to an attorney and the County Clerk.

The County Clerk accepts a deed only with several forms built in its online PREP system:

  • A Recording and Endorsement Cover Page
  • The state transfer tax return, Form TP-584
  • The Real Property Transfer Report, Form RP-5217
  • A Payment Cover Page with recording fees and tax

State transfer tax is $2 for each $500 of price, rounded up to the next $500. The Westchester clerk's own example shows a $404,501 price rounded to $405,000 and taxed at $1,620. The seller normally pays it. The one percent mansion tax on residences of $1 million or more is the buyer's cost under the state's rules. Ask your closing attorney for the exact figures on your own deed.

sections.h2: What permits or certificates can hold up a New Rochelle sale?
sections.html:
Open permits and a missing certificate of occupancy are the usual snags. The city says building permits are a New York State requirement, and it now takes permit applications through an online system. You do not need a permit to paint a house outside the Historical district, resurface a driveway without enlarging it, or put siding over existing sheathing on a one or two-family house.

If a prior owner finished a deck, attic or basement without closing the permit, the buyer's attorney will ask for the paperwork. A cash buyer purchasing as-is may take the house with those gaps, but expect the price to reflect them. Ask the city's building permit office what is open on your address before you list or accept any offer.

Homeowners who receive the STAR credit should also close that registration with the state when they sell, and the buyer registers at the Homeowner Benefit Portal once the new home is a primary residence.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in New Rochelle?
faqs.a: Four bills arrive each year, from the city, Westchester County, and the school and library taxes in two halves. City taxes are due January 31 and county taxes June 30.

faqs.q: Can I sell a New Rochelle house with open building permits?
faqs.a: Yes, but the buyer inherits the problem, so expect a lower offer or a request to close the permits first. Ask the city's building permit office which applications are open on your address before you accept an offer.

faqs.q: When is Grievance Day in New Rochelle?
faqs.a: It falls on the third Tuesday in February, after the February 1 tentative roll. The exemption application deadline is December 1, and the final roll is set on April 1.

faqs.q: Where is a New Rochelle deed recorded?
faqs.a: At the Westchester County Clerk, using forms created in the PREP system. The city assessor cannot change ownership records, so the deed and the TP-584 transfer tax return go to the county.

faqs.q: Does New Rochelle have a recent reassessment that could affect my price?
faqs.a: No citywide reassessment has been done since 1956, according to the assessor's office. Improvements are picked up individually as of December 1, so recent additions may raise a buyer's future bill.
